units.translation: while he himself is alive or dead
whether I speak of him dead or alive
for he was king while he lived
I mean killing the living and the dead
for even while living you considered him greater than your father
I seem to lament in vain, alive, at a tomb
living and dead
to drink from the living a red libation from their limbs
and having wasted you away while alive, I will take you below
and you will feast on me alive
therefore you are alive
why did you not drive her out while she was alive?
alive, I honor you with laments
lament me, the living, more than the dead
for what good is it to live a life that brings sorrows?
the whirlwinds of ruin are alive

Thus M, not ζεύγλησι, which is in some copies, where Hermann says: "ζεύγλην some say is the curvature of the yoke, others the part into which the neck of the beast is inserted, or, what is the same, the straps, which are called subiugia by the Latins. In this sense Aeschylus used it here, and before him Homer Il. 19, 405 πᾶσα δὲ χαίτη ζεύγλης ἐξεριποῦσα παρὰ ζυγὸν | οὐδας ἵκανεν. See the scholiasts on Homer and Scheffer on vehicular matters p. 116 ff."

and beneath the chariot he yokes them

and him who is not obedient I will yoke with heavy

The Doric form Ἀτρειδᾶν is foreign to these anapaests, whose origin seems to be traced back to the fact that Aeschylus used the dual number ζεῦγος ζεῦγος Ἀτρείδαιν, perhaps mindful of the Homeric Ἀτρείδα δὲ μάλιστα δύω, κοσμήτορε λαῶν. When this was easily mistaken for ΑΤΡΕΙΔΑN, the scribe wrote Ατρειδᾶν. The oldest example of this error is in Homer Il. 19, 310 where some manuscripts, including the Venetian A, have δοιώ δ᾽ Ἀτρείδαι μενέτην καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς, but the poet wrote what is in others Ἀτρείδα, as the dual numbers δοιώ and μενέτην require, and it is preserved in other places, such as Il. 1, 16. 385 Ἀτρείδα δὲ μάλιστα δύω, κοσμήτορε λαῶν, from which it does not follow, as Heynius thought, that in the same place v. 17 Ἀτρεῖδαί τε καὶ ἄλλοι ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί, or 8, 261 τὸν δὲ μέτ᾽ Ἀτρεῖδαι, Ἀγαμέμνων καὶ Μενέλαος, | τοῖσι δ᾽ ἐπ᾿ Αἴαντες etc. should be written Ἀτρείδα. For when no other dual noun is added, the plural is no less correct than 9, 341 ἢ μούνοι φιλέουσ᾽ ἀλόχους μερόπων ἀνθρώπων | Ἀτρείδαι, or Αἴαντες in the place just mentioned, although elsewhere he said Αἴαντε δύω. There is a different error in Photius p. 52, 20 ζεῦγος: τὸ ἐκ δυοῖν τινῶν ζευγνύμενον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ἐκ πλειόνων · καὶ γὰρ καὶ Ἰσοκράτης “τεθρίππων ζεῦγος” εἶπεν καὶ Αἰσχύλος “ζεῦγος τεθρίππων.” Omitting the name of Aeschylus, Etym.
